title: The Battle for the Independent Pharmacy
summary: Nimble CEO Talha Sattar calls on independent pharmacies to share evidence of CVS Health’s anticompetitive software blockades and weaponized audits to support federal investigations and defend their right to innovate.
body_text: The House Judiciary Committee has pulled back the curtain on what independent pharmacies have known for years: CVS Health is using its power to choke off competition. ‍ This isn’t a business disagreement. It’s a warning shot to every independent pharmacy that dares to modernize without permission. ‍ At stake is something fundamental: the right to compete, innovate, and serve patients without being punished by a dominant incumbent. ‍ The Goliath Playbook: Control the Market, Then the Rules ‍ CVS isn’t winning by building better tools. They’re winning by making sure no one else is allowed to use them. According to the House Judiciary Committee, CVS has launched a coordinated campaign on three fronts: ‍ 🔨 Weaponized Audits So-called “fraud” investigations used as intimidation tactics against pharmacies that adopt modern technology. ‍ 🧱 The Software Blockade Provider manuals rewritten to ban competitive software — forcing independents back into outdated, inefficient systems. ‍ 📜 Contractual Strong-Arming Cease-and-desist letters delivering a blunt ultimatum: Drop non-CVS approved solutions — or lose access to your patients. ‍ Let’s be clear: This isn’t oversight. It’s economic coercion. ‍ Why Nimble Stands with Independent Pharmacies ‍ CVS’s endgame is obvious: a healthcare system where they own the insurance, the technology, the payments, and the patient relationship. Independent pharmacies are allowed to exist — but never to compete. ‍ Nimble was built to break that model. We believe independent pharmacies deserve the same digital tools as anyone else — not permission slips, not threats, and not punishment for innovation. ‍ “If a company can decide which technology you’re allowed to use, you’re not a partner — you’re a captive.” ‍ That’s the line CVS doesn’t want discussed. ‍ This Is the Moment to Speak ‍ The investigation has started — but investigations don’t create change on their own. Change happens when the people impacted go on the record. If you’ve experienced any of the following, your story matters: ‍ Excessive or targeted audits Threatening letters tied to your technology choices Pressure to switch to CVS-approved software for payments, refills, or operations This isn’t complaining. This is documenting a pattern. ‍ “Silence is what turns abuse into policy.” ‍ Now is the moment independent pharmacies decide whether the rules will keep being written about them — or with them in mind. ‍ 📩 Reach out directly: Share your documentation and experiences with me at talha.sattar@nimblerx.com . ‍ Your voice is the leverage. Your evidence is how we force a level playing field — for every independent pharmacy in the country and the 75M+ Americans that use them every year. ‍ Talha Sattar CEO, NimbleRx

title: In the Surf
summary: We examine the brain injuries in the Coast Guard.
body_text: Advertisement SKIP ADVERTISEMENT You have a preview view of this article while we are checking your access. When we have confirmed access, the full article content will load. President Trump said his “Board of Peace” had reached a disarmament deal in Gaza . “For the first time, Hamas officially has committed to an actionable plan for relinquishing all its weapons, which will be followed by Israeli withdrawal from Gaza,” the board said. Neither side commented publicly. We have more news below. I’m going to start with the United States Coast Guard. Image Dave Philipps, who covers the United States military and veterans for The Times, has spent the past few years focused on the brain injuries suffered by members of elite and specialized units. He’s written about artillery crews who repeatedly fire high-powered cannons and about SEALs who do the same with shoulder-fired rockets. He’s written about what happens to the brains of fighter pilots who catapult from aircraft carriers, and to those of fast-boat crews who pound across the ocean. And now he’s turned his attention to the crews of Coast Guard rescue boats , who work and train in heavy, crashing seas in order to save lives. They’re called surfmen, and their work is among the most challenging and dangerous jobs in the service. It is work that comes at a cost, Dave reports. They take a beating from the ocean. Many veteran surfmen experience headaches, memory lapses, anxiety attacks, nightmares, mood swings and cognitive problems that can be symptoms of brain injuries. “A 20-foot wave breaking on you is like being in a car crash,” a surfman named Aaron Harris told him. “If you are out training in big surf, that’s like 20 car accidents a day.” Harris was on the boats for 22 years, before retiring in 2024. The surfmen are alone, Dave discovered. The Coast Guard has no regular testing protocol for brain injuries. It delivers no formal briefings on the dangers of pounding waves. The website it maintains on brain injuries is more than 10 years old. Dave found that many of the links that appear under a heading reading “Where to get help” are inactive. The surfmen suffer, and their families suffer, and the results can be fatal. Brett Bonner, 1982-2025 Image Brett Bonner served in the U.S. Coast Guard for 21 years. Credit... title: Cómo organizar tus pagos mensuales desde una sola plataforma y ahorrar tiempo
summary: ¿Deseas simplificar la gestión de tus finanzas? Aprende cómo organizar tus pagos mensuales desde una sola plataforma.
body_text: ¡Ahora puedes solicitar tu crédito por whatsapp! Sin papeleos ni complicaciones Pídelo ahora Administrar las finanzas personales parece una tarea sencilla cuando se observan los gastos de forma individual. Sin embargo, cuando comienzan a acumularse las obligaciones mensuales, la situación puede volverse más compleja de lo que parece. Servicios públicos, internet, telefonía móvil, plataformas de entretenimiento, créditos, seguros, arriendos, cuotas educativas y otros compromisos financieros forman parte de la realidad de millones de colombianos. Cada pago tiene una fecha diferente, un monto específico y, en muchos casos, un canal distinto para realizarlo. El resultado suele ser una sensación constante de desorden financiero. Muchas personas olvidan fechas de vencimiento, realizan pagos tarde o pierden visibilidad sobre cuánto dinero están gastando realmente cada mes. Para suerte de muchos, la transformación digital ha permitido que cada vez más usuarios puedan centralizar la administración de sus finanzas desde una sola plataforma. Esta tendencia no solo facilita el control de los gastos, sino que también ayuda a ahorrar tiempo, reducir errores y tomar mejores decisiones financieras. La llegada de nuevas herramientas digitales y sistemas de pagos más ágiles está permitiendo que la gestión del dinero sea mucho más sencilla que hace algunos años. Hoy es posible revisar movimientos, realizar pagos y monitorear obligaciones desde dispositivos móviles, sin necesidad de utilizar múltiples aplicaciones o procesos complejos. En este artículo descubrirás cómo centralizar tus pagos puede ayudarte a mejorar tu organización financiera, qué herramientas seguras existen para lograrlo y cómo plataformas como MONET pueden contribuir a una administración más eficiente de tus recursos. Ventajas de centralizar tus pagos y movimientos financieros en un solo lugar Uno de los principales desafíos financieros actuales es la dispersión de la información. Muchas personas administran su dinero utilizando diferentes canales para distintas necesidades. Una aplicación para transferencias, otra para pagos de servicios, otra para revisar movimientos bancarios y varias más para gestionar otros productos financieros. Aunque cada herramienta puede ser útil de forma individual, manejar demasiadas plataformas suele generar desorden. Centralizar los pagos y movimientos financieros ofrece múltiples beneficios. Mayor visibilidad sobre tus finanzas Cuando toda la información se encuentra concentrada en un mismo entorno, resulta mucho más fácil entender cómo se mueve el dinero. Puedes identificar con mayor claridad: Cuáles son tus gastos fijos. Cuáles son tus gastos variables. Cuánto dinero estás destinando a obligaciones financieras. Qué categorías consumen una mayor parte de tus ingresos. Esta visibilidad facilita la toma de decisiones y mejora la planificación financiera. Menos tiempo invertido en tareas administrativas Realizar consultas en múltiples aplicaciones o portales puede consumir tiempo innecesario. Una gestión centralizada reduce la necesidad de cambiar constantemente entre diferentes plataformas. Mejor organización financiera Tener acceso a toda la información desde un solo lugar ayuda a mantener un mayor orden y reduce la posibilidad de pasar por alto obligaciones importantes. Mayor control del flujo de dinero La centralización permite monitorear ingresos y gastos de forma más eficiente, facilitando el seguimiento de los recursos disponibles. Menor riesgo de errores Cuando la información está dispersa, aumentan las probabilidades de duplicar pagos, olvidar obligaciones o cometer equivocaciones durante las operaciones financieras. Por estas razones, cada vez más personas buscan soluciones que les permitan simplificar la administración de sus finanzas. Cómo tener mayor control sobre gastos recurrentes y fechas de pago Uno de los aspectos más importantes de una buena salud financiera es el control de los gastos recurrentes. Muchas obligaciones se repiten mes a mes: Servicios públicos. Telefonía móvil. Internet. Plataformas de entretenimiento. Seguros. Créditos. Cuotas educativas. Arriendos. Aunque cada pago puede parecer manejable por separado, la suma de todos ellos puede afectar significativamente el presupuesto mensual. Identifica todos tus compromisos financieros El primer paso consiste en elaborar una lista completa de todas las obligaciones recurrentes. Muchas personas se sorprenden al descubrir cuántos pagos realizan cada mes. Clasifica tus gastos Una forma útil de organizar la información es dividir los gastos en categorías: Vivienda. Transporte. Alimentación. Educación. Entretenimiento. Servicios. Créditos. Esto permite identificar áreas donde existen oportunidades de mejora. Registra las fechas de vencimiento Conocer exactamente cuándo debe realizarse cada pago ayuda a evitar retrasos y cargos adicionales. Programa recordatorios Las alertas digitales pueden convertirse en grandes aliadas para cumplir oportunamente con las obligaciones. Monitorea los cambios Algunos servicios pueden modificar sus tarifas con el tiempo. Revisar periódicamente los montos ayuda a mantener el presupuesto actualizado. La combinación de organización y seguimiento constante permite mantener un mayor control sobre las finanzas personales. Herramientas digitales que facilitan la administración de tus finanzas personales La tecnología ha transformado profundamente la forma en que administramos el dinero. Actualmente existen numerosas herramientas diseñadas para ayudar a los usuarios a organizar sus finanzas de manera más eficiente, siempre y cuando conozcamos con antelación cómo funcionan estas plataformas antes de hacer uso de ellas. Aplicaciones financieras Muchas aplicaciones permiten visualizar movimientos, registrar gastos y monitorear el comportamiento financiero desde el celular. Plataformas de pagos digitales Facilitan la realización de transferencias y pagos sin necesidad de acudir físicamente a una oficina o entidad financiera. Calendarios financieros Algunas herramientas permiten programar alertas relacionadas con fechas importantes y vencimientos. Reportes automáticos Los resúmenes de actividad financiera ayudan a comprender mejor cómo se utilizan los recursos económicos. Herramientas de seguimiento presupuestal Permiten establecer límites de gasto y monitorear el cumplimiento de objetivos financieros. El principal beneficio de estas soluciones es que reducen la carga operativa asociada a la administración del dinero, permitiendo que las personas dediquen más tiempo a otras actividades importantes. Además, una mayor visibilidad financiera suele traducirse en mejores decisiones económicas. Cómo reducir olvidos, retrasos y errores en tus obligaciones financieras Luego de solicitar un crédito , olvidar un pago puede parecer un incidente menor, pero cuando ocurre de forma repetida puede generar consecuencias importantes. Los retrasos pueden derivar en: Intereses de mora. Cargos adicionales. Deterioro del historial crediticio. Estrés financiero innecesario. Por eso, implementar estrategias para minimizar errores es una decisión inteligente. Automatiza cuando sea posible Los pagos automáticos ayudan a reducir el riesgo de olvidar fechas importantes. Mantén un calendario financiero Visualizar todas las obligaciones en un mismo lugar facilita la planificación. Revisa tus movimientos regularmente Dedicar algunos minutos cada semana a revisar tus finanzas permite detectar inconsistencias antes de que se conviertan en problemas mayores. Evita acumular demasiadas obligaciones Entre más compromisos financieros existan, mayor será la complejidad de la gestión. Conserva un margen de liquidez Mantener recursos disponibles para cubrir gastos inesperados ayuda a evitar incumplimientos. Utiliza herramientas digitales confiables Las soluciones tecnológicas pueden simplificar significativamente la administración de pagos y movimientos financieros. La prevención suele ser mucho más efectiva que la corrección de errores una vez ocurren. Cómo Monet te ayuda a simplificar la gestión de pagos mensuales La evolución de los servicios financieros digitales ha permitido que las personas administren sus recursos de forma más cómoda y eficiente. MONET, al ser una fintech confiable , forma parte de una nueva generación de plataformas orientadas a simplificar la experiencia financiera de los usuarios. Actualmente, muchas personas buscan herramientas que les permitan realizar diferentes operaciones desde el celular sin necesidad de recurrir a múltiples procesos o plataformas independientes. La tendencia hacia la centralización financiera responde precisamente a esa necesidad. Contar con una visión más clara de los movimientos financieros facilita: La planificación de gastos. El seguimiento de obligaciones. El control del presupuesto. La toma de decisiones económicas. Además, el avance de tecnologías como los pagos digitales y los sistemas de transferencias inmediatas está contribuyendo a que la administración financiera sea cada vez más sencilla y accesible. Plataformas como MONET se desarrollan dentro de este ecosistema moderno, donde la facilidad de uso, la organización y la eficiencia son aspectos cada vez más valorados por los usuarios. Más allá de la herramienta utilizada, el objetivo principal sigue siendo ayudar a las personas a mantener una relación más ordenada y saludable con su dinero. Preguntas frecuentes ¿Por qué es recomendable centralizar mis pagos en una sola plataforma? Porque facilita el control financiero, reduce errores, mejora la visibilidad sobre los gastos y permite administrar las obligaciones de manera más eficiente. ¿Qué gastos debería incluir en mi planificación mensual? Es recomendable incluir todos los gastos recurrentes, como servicios públicos, créditos, seguros, transporte, alimentación, educación y entretenimiento. ¿Los recordatorios realmente ayudan a evitar retrasos? Sí. Las alertas y recordatorios son herramientas muy efectivas para cumplir con las fechas de pago y evitar olvidos. ¿Cómo puedo mejorar la organización de mis finanzas personales? Manteniendo un registro actualizado de ingresos y gastos, utilizando herramientas digitales, programando recordatorios y revisando periódicamente tus movimientos financieros. En conclusión: La organización financiera no depende únicamente de cuánto dinero ganas, sino también de cómo administras tus obligaciones y recursos cada mes. Centralizar pagos y movimientos financieros en una sola plataforma puede ayudarte a ahorrar tiempo, reducir errores y tener una visión mucho más clara de tu situación económica. Además, facilita el seguimiento de gastos recurrentes y permite tomar decisiones más informadas. Las herramientas digitales actuales ofrecen oportunidades valiosas para simplificar la administración financiera y mejorar la experiencia de los usuarios. Plataformas como MONET forman parte de esta evolución, ayudando a que la gestión del dinero sea más práctica y accesible.

title: What is B2B sales? Definition, process & strategies
summary: What B2B sales is, how it differs from B2C, the process stages, and the roles that drive deals.
body_text: TL;DR B2B sales is when one business sells products or services to another business, closing deals through demos, proposals, and negotiation with decision-makers. Unlike B2C, where an individual buys on impulse, B2B deals carry higher contract values, involve several stakeholders, and take longer to close because buyers need to justify the return on investment. A typical B2B sales process moves through six stages, from prospecting and qualification through needs assessment, proposal, negotiation, and close, then continues into account management after the sale. The work spans dedicated roles, including sales development reps who prospect, account executives who close, and account managers who retain and grow customers. For SMB and growth-stage teams, understanding this process matters because accurate prospect data and a repeatable pipeline directly determine how many deals you win. What B2B sales means in practice B2B sales happens when one business sells its product or service to another business rather than to an individual consumer. A software company selling a payroll platform to a 200-person manufacturer, a wholesaler supplying inventory to a chain of restaurants, an agency landing a year-long retainer with a growing brand. In each case, the buyer is an organization spending organizational money, and that single fact reshapes everything about how the deal moves. Three traits define the shape of almost every B2B deal. The contracts carry high value and often recur, which means both sides treat the purchase as a real commitment. Salesforce notes that some transactions "can run into the millions of dollars," and switching costs push buyers to stay for years ( Salesforce ). Multiple stakeholders weigh in, from mid-level managers up to the C-suite, each with a different agenda. Because more people and money are involved, the close takes longer, often stretching across weeks or months of demos, proposals, and negotiation. Compare that to how a consumer buys. Someone sees a sweatshirt in an Instagram ad, likes it, and checks out in under a minute. Nobody circulates the decision for approval or builds a business case for a candy bar at the register. B2C sales run on individual impulse and a short path to purchase. B2B buyers move the opposite way. Before a company adopts, say, an AI tool for hundreds of employees, someone has to justify the cost, prove the return, and win agreement from every team the change touches. The buyer needs to understand the ROI before signing, so the seller's job is to educate and de-risk the decision rather than trigger a quick yes. That single difference, buying on justified ROI instead of impulse, explains most of what follows in a B2B process. How B2B sales differs from B2C sales The clearest way to separate B2B from B2C sales is to look at three things: how much money changes hands, how many people approve the purchase, and how long the whole thing takes. Consumer sales run small, fast, and personal. Business sales run large, slow, and collective. Those differences reshape how a rep has to sell. Deal size sets the tone. A shopper impulse-buys a sweatshirt from an Instagram ad without a second thought, but a business buying AI software for hundreds of employees commits thousands of dollars and locks in switching costs for years. B2B contracts can run into the millions , so buyers move carefully. Decision-maker count is the next axis. A consumer decides alone at the checkout line. A B2B purchase pulls in mid-level managers through the C-suite, each with a different agenda, and the deal stalls until every stakeholder is satisfied. A rep who wins over one champion still loses if finance or IT blocks the deal later. Cycle length follows directly from the first two axes. More money and more approvers mean more presentations, demos, and negotiations, which stretch the timeline from days to months. Those three differences change the rep's actual job. In B2C, the sale rides on impulse and emotion, so a strong ad and an easy checkout do most of the work. In B2B, the buyer needs to understand ROI before signing, so the rep spends the cycle educating stakeholders, quantifying value, and answering objections from people who never spoke to each other. You are not closing a mood. You are building a case that survives review by a committee. The B2B sales process, stage by stage Most B2B deals move through seven stages, and knowing where a prospect sits tells you what work comes next. The exact shape varies by company size and deal complexity, but the underlying logic holds for nearly every SMB and growth-stage team. A one-person shop selling a $500 subscription touches the same stages as an enterprise closing a seven-figure contract. The larger deal just spends longer in each one. Stage What happens Typical owner Prospecting and lead generation Identify companies that fit the buyer profile SDR, marketing Lead qualification Confirm budget, authority, need, and timing SDR, AE Needs assessment Uncover the specific problem and internal pressures AE Proposal and quote Present a tailored solution tied to discovery AE Negotiation Work out price, terms, and implementation scope AE, procurement Close Finalize the contract and hand off to onboarding AE Account management and expansion Retain, renew, and grow the account CSM, account manager Prospecting and lead generation You start by finding companies that could plausibly buy. Sales and marketing identify potential customers through ads, inbound signups, and research-based outreach that targets a defined buyer profile. The quality of this stage sets a ceiling on everything after it, because a pipeline full of poor-fit accounts wastes every hour that follows. Lead qualification Next, you separate the accounts worth pursuing from the ones that aren't. Reps assess product fit against budget, authority, need, and timing before investing serious effort. A qualified lead has a real problem your product solves and someone who can approve the spend. Needs assessment Once a prospect qualifies, you uncover what they actually need. Reps run discovery calls to map the specific problems, current tools, and internal pressures driving the search. Skip this and every later pitch aims at a target you can't see. Proposal and quote You then present a tailored solution built around what discovery revealed. The proposal ties your product to the prospect's stated problems and puts a price on the outcome. A generic quote signals you weren't listening, so the strongest proposals reference the buyer's own language. Negotiation Here you work out the terms, covering price, contract length, implementation scope, and anything the buyer's procurement team flags. Multiple stakeholders often surface at this point with competing priorities, so expect the deal to slow while people reach agreement internally. Close You finalize and process the sale details, sign the contract, and hand off to whoever owns onboarding. Closing rate against everything that reached this stage is one of the clearest signals of how well the earlier work held up. Account management and expansion The relationship continues after the signature, and for most B2B companies that's where the real revenue lives. An account owner nurtures the customer through renewals, upsells, and cross-sells over the life of the contract. Because switching costs keep B2B buyers in place for years, a retained account that expands each renewal often outweighs a new logo won this quarter. Neglect this stage and you refill the top of the funnel just to replace customers you already had. Who's involved: common B2B sales roles A B2B sale usually passes through several hands, and each role owns a specific stage of the deal. Understanding that handoff chain makes the job titles far less confusing than they first appear. The chain starts with a sales development rep (SDR) , who owns the top of the funnel. An SDR spends the day prospecting and qualifying, sending cold outreach, and booking meetings. Their goal is not to close anything but to find leads worth a real conversation and hand them off warm. An account executive (AE) takes the qualified lead and runs the deal from there. The AE handles needs assessment, demos, proposals, and negotiation, and carries a quota tied to closed revenue. When people say a rep "owns the number," they usually mean the AE. After the contract signs, the customer moves to a customer success manager (CSM) or account manager . A CSM focuses on adoption and retention, making sure the customer actually gets value so they renew. An account manager leans more toward growing the relationship through upsells and expansion. Some companies split these two jobs, and others combine them into one post-sale owner. A sales manager sits above the SDRs and AEs rather than inside the deal flow. The manager coaches reps, forecasts pipeline, and decides where the team spends its time. Their metric is the performance of the group, not any single deal. At an SMB or early growth-stage company, one person often plays several of these roles at once. A founder or first sales hire might prospect, demo, close, and manage the account through renewal, all without a formal title. The handoff chain still describes the work that has to happen, even when the same person does every part of it. As headcount grows, teams tend to peel off the SDR function first, then split success and account management from the AE, because specialization at each stage lets reps do more of what they are best at. Role Owns Primary metric SDR Prospecting and qualifying, booking meetings Meetings booked AE Needs assessment through close Closed revenue CSM / account manager Adoption, retention, upsells after close Renewal rate, expansion revenue Sales manager Coaching, forecasting, pipeline oversight Team performance Metrics that show whether a B2B sales process is working Five numbers tell you whether your process is healthy, and each one maps back to a stage the prospect moves through. Track them together, because a strong result in one metric often hides a weakness in another. Win rate measures how many qualified opportunities you close. Divide closed-won deals by the total number of qualified opportunities in a period, and you get a percentage that reflects the quality of your qualification stage. A rising win rate usually means your reps are disqualifying poor-fit prospects earlier rather than chasing every lead. A falling one often signals that unqualified deals are slipping deep into the pipeline before dying. Sales cycle length tracks how long a deal takes from first qualified touch to close. Long cycles are normal in B2B, since deals cross multiple stakeholders and require ROI justification. What matters is where time accumulates. If deals sit for weeks in the proposal or negotiation stage, that dwell time points to a specific bottleneck rather than a vague slowdown, and you can attack it directly. Average deal size tells you the typical revenue per closed deal in a given period. Watch the trend against your win rate. A shrinking average deal size alongside a rising win rate often means your team is closing easier, smaller deals and avoiding the larger, harder ones. Annual Contract Value, or ACV, captures the average revenue a customer contract generates over a year. Salesforce defines it as the average sales amount of a contract across twelve months. ACV matters more than a one-time deal figure when you sell subscriptions or recurring services, because it reflects the revenue you can count on year over year. Customer Lifetime Value, or CLV, measures the total value a customer generates across the full relationship, including upsells, cross-sells, and renewals. A healthy CLV climbing over time signals that your account management stage is working and that customers expand rather than churn. When CLV stalls while you keep winning new logos, the problem lives after the close, not before it. Common challenges in B2B sales Most B2B deals stall not because the product is wrong, but because too many people have to agree before anyone signs. A single purchase can touch a mid-level manager, a department head, and a C-suite budget owner, and each of them weighs a different concern. One cares about implementation time, another about cost, another about how the tool fits next year's plan. A newer rep often sells hard to one enthusiastic contact, only to watch the deal die when a stakeholder they never spoke to raises an objection. Long cycles create a second, quieter problem. Because complex deals take months to close, a rep's pipeline can look full while producing almost no revenue for a quarter. Deals sit in negotiation, decision-makers go quiet, and forecasts drift. A pipeline that stalls in the middle stages is harder to diagnose than one that never fills, because the activity looks healthy right up until the numbers come in short. The friction that wastes the most effort, though, starts before any of that. Reps burn hours reaching contacts who left the company, calling numbers that no longer connect, or pitching a business that was never a fit in the first place. Bad contact and company data quietly poisons every stage downstream. You qualify against a wrong headcount, you personalize outreach to the wrong owner, and you build a proposal around assumptions that were never true. For a closer look at how this plays out stage by stage, see what sales prospecting actually involves . Data quality sits underneath most of these problems as a root cause, not a side issue. When the underlying records about a prospect and their business are accurate, stakeholder mapping, qualification, and outreach all get easier. When they are wrong, no amount of process discipline saves the deal. Where accurate prospect and company data fits in Accurate prospect data determines whether the first two stages of the process work at all. Customer research means building an ideal buyer profile before you reach out, and outreach means contacting the right person through the right channel. Both collapse when the underlying records are wrong. A rep who dials a disconnected number or emails a manager who left two years ago wastes the same effort that could have moved a live deal forward. The problem gets worse for teams selling to small and local businesses, because public data on them is thin. A national enterprise publishes its executives, filings, and org structure. A regional clinic, restaurant, or contractor rarely does. The owner who actually signs the deal often does not appear in the standard databases built around employees at large companies, so reps end up guessing at names and addresses. Good data also carries through to account management. When you know the owner, their location, and their category from the start, qualification and post-sale nurturing rest on facts rather than assumptions. How to use SMB intelligence for data-driven sales prioritization covers how that data feeds directly into which accounts a rep works first. Tools like Openmart exist to close that gap for SMB prospecting, surfacing verified owner and company contact details at small businesses that most databases miss. Reliable inputs at the top of the funnel mean fewer bounced emails, cleaner pipeline, and time spent on prospects who can actually buy. FAQs What is B2B sales in simple terms? B2B sales is when one business sells products or services to another business rather than to individual consumers. A software company selling project management tools to a marketing agency is running a B2B sale. The buyer purchases to solve a business problem, so the seller has to prove a return before the deal closes. How is B2B sales different from B2C? B2C sales target individual shoppers who often buy quickly, like someone grabbing a candy bar at a checkout line. B2B sales involve larger deal sizes, several decision-makers, and a longer cycle because the buyer needs to justify the spend to their team. As a result, B2B reps sell through education and ROI evidence rather than impulse. What are the stages of a B2B sales process? Most B2B processes move through prospecting, lead qualification, needs assessment, proposal, negotiation, and close. After the sale, an account team handles onboarding, retention, and expansion. Every company adjusts the shape, but that sequence holds for most SMB and growth-stage teams. What roles make up a B2B sales team? A common structure includes an SDR who prospects, an account executive who runs demos and closes, and an account manager or customer success manager who owns the relationship after the sale. A sales manager oversees the team and tracks performance. Smaller companies often collapse several of these roles into one person. What is a good win rate or sales cycle length for B2B? Win rate and cycle length vary widely by industry and deal size, so measure your own trend rather than chasing a fixed number. A win rate holding steady or climbing while cycles shorten signals a healthy process.

title: Interns of Expedia Group 2026: Meet the Design Builders
summary: We empower you to discover a world of growth and potential, so you can help travelers explore the world, one journey at a time..
body_text: This summer, Expedia Group welcomed our first ever Design Builder interns to our teams in Seattle and London. More than a traditional internship, the Design Builder Internship program is designed for emerging product designers who will shape not only how experiences look, but also how they work—bringing together craft, systems thinking, and AI-native design practices. As they settle in, connect with fellow Expedians, and jump into hands-on work across our travel portfolio, we took a moment to get to know them. Hear about what drew them to this opportunity and what they’re most excited to explore as they help bring new ideas to life. Rida Merchant | University of Leicester | Hotels.com Design Team | London Why did you decide to join Expedia Group? Having traveled to 8 countries, I’ve experienced some of the challenges travelers face first-hand – finding genuine value, understanding what a deal actually includes, and discovering places I might not have considered before. Joining EG gave me the opportunity to work on these kinds of problems at a global scale, helping millions of travelers across different markets and cultures. What excites me most is the opportunity to explore how AI can be integrated into the design process – not just as an add-on, but as part of how we design, build and evaluate our work. As an intern, it’s exciting to be able to contribute to and learn in a space that is evolving so quickly. What do you want to achieve by the end of the program? There are two things I’d love to achieve. First, I want to become more confident and fluent in AI-native design workflows. I think understanding how to work effectively with AI will be an important skill for the next generation of designers, and I want to explore how it can genuinely improve the way we work. Secondly, I want to meet and learn from as many people as possible. One of the best parts of a program like this is being surrounded by designers, researchers and fellow interns across different teams and brands, and I’d love to leave with relationships that continue well beyond the summer. What are some activities you enjoy outside of work ? Traveling, unsurprisingly – 8 countries so far and counting! Cappadocia in Turkey has definitely been my favorite so far. I love experiencing new places, cultures and food. Mark Tsang | Nottingham Trent University | Expedia Landing Design Team | London Why did I decide to join EG? I came from a very different design background (Industrial/Graphic) and thought I could apply that type of design thinking onto this role at EG. Working in such a big company in house and focusing on these small elements shows how much thought is put into each piece of design before it is shipped out to the customer! What do I want to achieve by the end of the program? I hope to understand the Experience Design space more and to have a grasp on what it’s like to work in such a big company! What do you like to do for fun? I love to play badminton and often go cafe hopping. The biggest coffee and matcha enthusiast! Junjin Tan | University of Michigan | Design System Team | Seattle Why did you decide to join EG? What really drew me to Expedia Group was the scale of the design department. One of my very first experiences as an intern was attending the Experience Design Town Hall, and seeing hundreds of designers from around the world actively collaborating and discussing what they’ve worked on to push travel experiences forward was genuinely unlike anything I’d seen before. That impression only deepened once I started working with my team; the depth behind the design system reflects an organization that prioritizes design as an infrastructure. What do you want to achieve by the end of the program? Interning at a company like Expedia Group is a rare opportunity and being immersed in a corporate design ecosystem with guidelines and systems as mature as my team has already taught me more than I expected. For me, this internship is about bridging the gap between coursework and reality; taking concepts I’ve explored in class and seeing them actually come to life in prototypes that real teams use and build on. By the end of the program, I want to walk away with a body of work that reflects what I’ve learned from collaborating with and being around designers who are much further along in their careers than I am. What do you like to do for fun? Since moving to Washington I’ve been leaning into the outdoors a lot more — hiking, pickleball, and rock climbing have all become regulars, and on Thursdays a group of us interns get together for volleyball and spikeball on the lawn. Outside of that I play saxophone, paint, and read. Brenda Yang | New York University | AI Shopping & Group Trip Planning Team | Seattle Why did you decide to join EG? My first impression of the program was that it felt more cross-functional than a typical design internship. I liked how closely it works with product, engineering, and AI, and I was especially drawn to the way my team values shipping work that I’m genuinely excited about. What do you want to achieve by the end of the program? I want to deepen my understanding of AI shopping in a travel context and create a meaningful project for my portfolio! What do you like to do for fun? I love to go on hikes, play pickleball, and attend concerts.
